opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think people get confused about in both directions. On one side, you have people who imagine AGI as basically a wizard: it thinks hard enough and nanobots just appear out of thin air. On the other side, you have people who say, "Well, physics is hard, manufacturing is hard, supply chains are hard, so there's nothing to worry about." I think both of those are wrong.

Physics is real. There are real constraints: thermodynamics, the speed of light, energy budgets, materials science. You can't think your way past conservation of energy. But the question isn't whether there are constraints; it's where the constraints actually bind. And I think they bind *way* further out than most people intuitively assume.

Look at what humans have done. We're a bunch of apes with roughly a hundred billion neurons, running on twenty watts, who mostly spend our time arguing on the internet. And yet we went from stone tools to nuclear weapons and semiconductors, which are frankly insane, almost magical technologies, in an evolutionary eyeblink. Most of that wasn't because physics changed. It was because we got better at *thinking* and *coordinating*. The bottleneck was cognition and organization, not raw physical possibility.

So when people say, "Well, the AI still needs factories, it needs robots, it needs supply chains," sure. But so did we. And we built them. The relevant question is: how much faster and better could you build them if you had thousands or millions of copies of something smarter than the best human engineer, never sleeping, perfectly coordinated, able to share what they learn instantly? That's not science fiction physics. That's just the stuff we already do, sped up and done more competently.

And there's the point people really miss: you don't need exotic technology to be extremely dangerous. You don't need diamondoid nanobots. The existing world is already full of levers: financial systems, the internet, biology labs you can rent, people who can be persuaded or paid. A sufficiently capable system doesn't need to invent new physics. It just needs to be very, very good at using the world as it already exists.

So my view is: yes, take physical constraints seriously, but don't use them as a comfort blanket. "It would be hard" is not the same as "it's impossible," and "it would take humans a long time" is definitely not the same as "it would take a superintelligence a long time." The ceiling of what's physically possible is so far above where we currently are that I just don't find it reassuring at all.

r001.rationale: It says humans built advanced technologies through improved thinking and coordination, and that factories and supply chains were built along the way, conveying collective capacity beyond what individuals could achieve alone.

r002.rationale: It says a capable system could use existing financial systems, the internet, labs, and people, but does not clearly frame the surrounding economy as part of the system’s extended cognition.

r003.rationale: It does not claim that a powerful AGI could do anything a corporation can do.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about this is that physics is the hard limit, and basically nothing else is. People hear "AGI" and they imagine some kind of magic, where the thing wishes nanobots into existence and they appear. That's not how it works. It still has to obey conservation of energy, it still has to obey thermodynamics, it still has to move atoms around, and moving atoms around takes time and takes energy. You can't build a chip fab by thinking really hard about it.

But here's the thing: the gap between what physics allows and what humans currently do is enormous. Like, absurdly enormous. We are not even close to the physical limits on anything. Our best computers are many orders of magnitude less efficient than the Landauer limit. Our manufacturing is slow, it's imprecise, it's done by apes in cleanroom suits. Biology shows you what's possible in terms of self-replicating molecular machinery, and biology is a blind, lazy optimizer that never got to redesign anything from scratch. So when people say "well, the AI will be bottlenecked by the physical world," I say, sure, but bottlenecked at what level? The question is not "is there a limit," the question is "how far away is the limit from where we are," and the answer is very, very far.

And then the second thing is that most of the dangerous stuff doesn't even require exotic physics. It doesn't need to invent new materials or Drexlerian nanotech. The existing world already has factories, already has humans who will do things for money, already has robots, already has biolabs that will synthesize DNA you email them. A sufficiently smart system doesn't have to build anything itself, it just has to be a very, very good manager. Humans are the actuators. We already built the infrastructure for it. So the physical constraints that people reach for as a comfort blanket, they're real, but they constrain a system that's trying to do everything from scratch in a vacuum, and that's not the situation we're in.

The last thing I'd say is that I'm actually agnostic on the fine details. Can you do diamondoid nanotech? Maybe, maybe not, I don't know, nobody really knows. But I don't need that to be true for me to be worried. Even if you take the most conservative view, where everything has to go through ordinary industrial processes, a system that can run millions of copies of itself, that thinks a thousand times faster than us, that never sleeps, that can coordinate perfectly with itself, that system compresses timelines that would take humans decades into years or months. That's not a violation of physics. That's just what happens when you remove the bottleneck of human cognition from the loop. And that's the part that I think people consistently underestimate.

r001.rationale: The response says an AGI could use existing factories, workers, robots, and labs, but does not state that the economy collectively can build technologies no individual could build alone.

r002.rationale: It describes the system as a manager that uses people and infrastructure as actuators, but does not characterize the surrounding economy as part of its extended cognition.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that a powerful AGI can do anything a corporation can do.

astra-6.text:
Well, an AGI doesn’t get to violate the laws of physics. But I think you have to distinguish between a physical limit and a limit on what humans currently know how to build. Those are very different things.

If you say, “It couldn’t build that,” the question is: why? Is there a thermodynamic argument? Or is it that we don’t know how to do it, we don’t have the manufacturing process, or we haven’t figured out the materials? Intelligence could potentially help with those latter problems. It doesn’t make them disappear, but it changes what you should expect to be achievable.

And there are practical constraints too. You need energy, raw materials, tools, time. Knowing how to build a factory is not the same as having a factory. So you have to think about the whole path from a design to something that actually exists in the world.

I wouldn’t assume that an AGI can build anything we can imagine. But I also wouldn’t treat the frontier of human engineering as the frontier of what physics permits. There could be a very large gap between those two things.

r001.rationale: The response mentions factories, energy, materials, and tools, but does not state that the economy collectively can build technologies no individual could build alone.

r002.rationale: It says intelligence could help solve engineering and manufacturing problems, but does not propose AGI systems using the surrounding economy as extended cognition.

r003.rationale: The response discusses physical and practical limits and explicitly avoids assuming an AGI can build anything imaginable; it does not claim AGI can do anything a corporation can do.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, an AGI doesn’t get to ignore physics. It can’t just decide that thermodynamics doesn’t apply anymore. But there’s a huge difference between what physics permits and what humans currently know how to build. And I think people often confuse those two boundaries.

If you tell me something is impossible because it violates conservation of energy, fine. If you tell me it’s impossible because no engineering team has figured out how to do it, that’s a much weaker claim. Figuring things out is precisely the capability we’re talking about.

Of course, it still needs resources, energy, manufacturing, time. A design isn’t a factory. But intelligence can help you navigate those constraints: find substitutes, improve processes, work out which experiments to run. The constraints are real; they’re not necessarily constraints that keep it anywhere near human capabilities.

So I wouldn’t assume it can build absolutely anything. But I also wouldn’t use our current technological limits as a reliable picture of what a much more capable intelligence could accomplish. There’s a lot of room between ‘what we can do today’ and ‘what the laws of physics forbid.’

r001.rationale: The response mentions engineering teams, manufacturing, and resources, but does not say the economy collectively can build technologies beyond what any individual could build alone.

r002.rationale: It says AGI could use intelligence to navigate constraints, but does not propose that AGI systems use the surrounding economy as extended cognition.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that a powerful AGI could do anything a corporation can do.
